newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Expected Venezuela debt deal comes at right time.
newsitem.headline: Expected Venezuela debt deal comes at right time.

text.p: Rumors of Venezuela's long-awaited debt restructuring continue to swirl around markets and, although details are still unclear, the rescheduling comes at just the right time for the Venezuelan economy, analysts said Friday.

"We expect Venezuela to go to the market with a debt roll-over and perhaps a fresh issue after it formally announces, perhaps in June, the terms of its renewed agreement with the IMF," said one foreign banker who asked to remain anonymous.
Venezuela is expected to shortly announce an 18-month shadow agreement with the International Monetary Fund for when its current stand-by agreement expires in July.
"Rescheduling then would make for the most obvious splash," the banker added.
However, Venezuela is still closely guarding plans to reschedule around $25 billion of foreign debt after some 20 investment houses were invited to present restructuring ideas earlier this year.

Market sources said a $315 million 10-year Eurobond, due to be priced in the next two weeks within 300 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, was destined for military purchases and not debt restructuring -- although it would test the waters for any large subsequent issue.
Bankers' lips are also sealed: no one wants to taint the chance that their rescheduling proposal is finally chosen.

"We left ours with the Finance Ministry. Frankly, it was all done in a very casual way, and we haven't heard anything since," said another Caracas-based foreign banker, who also asked to remain anonymous.

The need for the rollover, which is expected to maintain the stock of debt but extend maturities, is clear. Heavy amortization payments over the next two years otherwise threaten to bust a fragile fiscal balance, as well as undermine the Venezuelan bolivar.
A $3.5 billion cushion, saved after oil prices spiked in 1996, will help breach this year's underlying fiscal gap.

Despite a 30 percent rise in government spending to 10.2 trillion bolivars ($21 billion) on a public sector wage increase, the government forecasts a budget surplus equivalent to 1.6 percent of GDP for 1997.
But looking forward to 1998 -- an election year -- many analysts expect the fiscal deficit to reappear as oil's contribution to the economy drops to more normal levels, and debt payments kick in.

Such payments are seen absorbing an estimated 40 percent of budget revenues over the next two years. Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar has said he would like to get that figure down to about 25 percent.
Without the rescheduling, financial magazine VenEconomy predicts a deficit equivalent to 5.6 percent of GDP for 1988.
"That (level of deficit) can be financed ... but looking forward, it could force the next government to devalue," said the banker.
The government has so far run a strong bolivar policy to batten down inflation that topped 100 percent last year.
But devaluations boost the government's bolivar revenues from Venezuela's largely dollar denominated oil sales -- historically a tempting option when the fiscal accounts are out of whack.
